newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia hopes to become BAe Hawk depot.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia hopes to become BAe Hawk depot.

text.p: Australia, having chosen the British Aerospace Hawk to fill an air force training requirement, hopes to become the regional maintenance depot for the hot-selling light attack aircraft.

"It's definitely a plus that there's the possibility that Australia can become the place where maintenance for other Hawks in the region can be done," Defence Industry Minister Bronwyn Bishop told reporters on Tuesday.
Australia is a relatively late customer for the Hawk.
British Aerospace has sold more than 700 copies of the aircraft to 15 air forces since it began building it for Britain's Royal Air Force in the 1970s.
Among Australia's neighbours, Malaysia has bought 28 and Indonesia 40. Brunei is expected to order 10 and South Korea has taken another 20.

But Australia plans to perform its own deep maintenance -- such as intensive overhauls -- rather than returning the aircraft to the supplier, as most customers do. It hopes to perform the same work for its neighbours.
Qantas Airways Ltd will maintain the Hawks' Rolls-Royce Adour engines in Sydney. The airframes will be handled by privately held Hunter Aerospace at Newcastle.
Bishop said the final number of Hawks in Australia's order would not be determined until the contract is signed in the second quarter of 1997. "It will be in excess of 30," she said.

The Defence Department had previously said up to 40 would be needed for its training requirement, but it wanted the contractor to determine the exact number. The two-seat Hawk was originally built as a trainer, but the latest Hawk 100 version has a full attack capability. -- Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2370
